messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Electrician
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Breathing): Heavy breathing sounds, Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociation: I pretend it happened to someone else, Counterfactual Thinking: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Vignette:
Anong is a 54-year-old electrician, a trade she has practiced with pride and precision for over thirty years. It has been nearly two years since the severe pneumonia that almost took her life, but the quiet confidence she once had in her own body has been replaced by a state of constant, vigilant alert. The event itself remains a series of fragmented sensory impressions. She remembers the initial struggle to breathe, a terrifying tightening in her chest that felt like a vise. The most vivid part is the sound: the ragged, wet gasps of her own lungs failing, a sound that seemed to come from outside of her, monstrous and unfamiliar. She recalls the sterile, chemical smell of the ambulance and the emergency room, an odor that clung to everything and promised only crisis. For three weeks in the ICU, much of it on a ventilator, that smell and the rhythmic whoosh of the machine were her entire world.

Upon returning home, the relief her family felt was not something Anong could fully share. Her body, once a reliable tool of her trade, now felt like a tripwire. She describes a persistent tension in her shoulders and jaw, a feeling of being perpetually braced for an impact that never comes. This physical readiness often outpaces her conscious thought. Last month, while wiring a new construction home, she was in a quiet attic space with her much younger apprentice. He had just hauled a heavy spool of wire up the ladder, and his heavy, strained breathing filled the small space. Before Anong even registered the sound consciously, her heart began to hammer against her ribs, a cold sweat breaking out across her forehead. She felt a dizzying wave of panic, a certainty that her own lungs were seizing up, and had to grip a rafter to keep from falling. Her body was reacting to a danger her mind couldn't see, replaying a threat that was two years in the past.

Over time, Anong developed ways to manage this constant state of threat. She began to meticulously avoid any reminder of her illness. She has not seen her primary care physician for a check-up since her hospital discharge, ignoring the clinic’s reminder calls. The sight of an ambulance on the road is enough to make her change her route, and she will leave a store if the smell of antiseptic cleaning products is too strong. When memories of the ICU do break through, she has a specific way of coping: she tells herself the story as if it happened to someone else. In her mind, it is not her in that bed, but “that woman,” a stranger whose suffering she can observe with a detached pity. This allows her to get through the day, but at night, she finds herself lost in thoughts of what might have been. She spends hours tracing the path of a different life, one in which she never got sick, never lost her strength, and never learned the intimate sound of her own body failing.

The second anniversary of her hospital admission passed last month, and the date itself loomed like a physical presence in her calendar. The week leading up to it was unbearable, filled with a free-floating dread and a return of the phantom breathlessness that sends her into a panic. The experience left her exhausted and feeling more disconnected than ever. It was this, coupled with her son’s persistent, worried questions about why she wouldn’t go for a simple physical exam, that finally prompted her to seek help. She has come to believe that her body is fundamentally untrustworthy, a fragile vessel that could betray her again at any moment. What frightens her most is this loss of self-reliance. She wants, more than anything, to be able to climb a ladder or hear a person catch their breath without her own body screaming that she is dying.
